publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Human Ventral Parietal Cortex Plays a Functional Role on Visuospatial Attention and Primary Consciousness. A Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Study

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: To our knowledge, this is the first direct experimental evidence of functional effects of bilateral ventral PPC on both visuospatial attention and primary consciousness.

span.label: visuospatial attention and primary visual consciousness
span.quote: In the present study, we wondered whether human ventral PPC plays a causal role on visuospatial attention and primary consciousness and whether these 2 functions are correlated with each other.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: In this paper, we used repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in 18 normal subjects to investigate whether the ventral posterior parietal cortex (PPC) plays a causal role on visuospatial attention and primary consciousness and whether these 2 functions are linearly correlated with each other.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: rTMS spreads transsynaptically into two networks whose interaction is nonlinear, so perturbing ventral PPC dissociates attention from consciousness instead of moving them together
span.quote: Interaction of these networks might be nonlinear and too complex to cause simple relationships between visuospatial attention and primary consciousness, at least due to the focal and week TMS-induced perturbation of ventral PPC.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a focal coil at near-threshold intensity limits the induced neural interference within a widely distributed network, which is why the behavioural effect is only about 10%
span.quote: The small but significant magnitude of rTMS effects on ventral PPC (about 10%) is likely due to the use of focal coil and near-threshold intensity of rTMS.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the stimulation disrupts the spatial disengagement operation of Posner's attention system, which then lengthens reaction time
span.quote: It is likely that the present rTMS of ventral PPC mainly effected spatial disengagement, in agreement with previous clinical studies showing that ventral PPC lesions are related to prominent spatial disengagement deficits

span.label: The behavioural effect of the stimulation was small, attributed to the focal coil and near-threshold intensity used.
span.note: what this limits: the SIZE of the reported effect: THE SMALL BUT SIGNIFICANT MAGNITUDE OF rTMS EFFECTS ON VENTRAL PPC (ABOUT 10%) IS LIKELY DUE TO THE USE OF FOCAL COIL AND NEAR-THRESHOLD INTENSITY OF rTMS
span.quote: The small but significant magnitude of rTMS effects on ventral PPC (about 10%) is likely due to the use of focal coil and near-threshold intensity of rTMS.

span.label: rTMS effects are not confined to the targeted region, so the locus of the effect is not purely ventral PPC.
span.note: what this limits: any claim that localises the effect to ventral PPC: THE EFFECT OF rTMS DOES NOT REMAIN LIMITED TO THE TARGETED BRAIN REGION BUT SPREAD TRANSYNAPTICALLY
span.quote: As a premise, it should be remarked that the effect of rTMS does not remain limited to the targeted brain region but spread transynaptically.

span.label: A motor-output contribution to the reaction-time slowing cannot be excluded.
span.note: what this limits: the reaction-time interpretation: THE SLOWING OF THE REACTION TIME IS MAINLY DUE TO VISUOSPATIAL SENSORY PROCESSING, ALTHOUGH A SLIGHT INFLUENCE ON MOTOR OUTPUT CANNOT BE EXCLUDED
span.quote: It is reasonable that the slowing of the reaction time is mainly due to visuospatial sensory processing, although a slight influence on motor output cannot be excluded.

span.label: The paper's consciousness measure is the percentage of trials a subject reported seeing.
span.note: what this limits: any citation of this paper as evidence about consciousness: trials associated with the conscious perception of the cue stimuli were defined as seen trials, and the reported measure is their percentage
span.quote: Trials associated with the conscious perception of cue stimuli were defined as ‘‘seen trials

span.label: The stimulus duration was calibrated per subject to about 50% detection, so the baseline rate is a design target.
span.note: what this limits: the baseline seen-trial rate reported here: the threshold time was defined as the cue duration producing about 50% of correct stimulus detections within a series of 10 trials, so a baseline near 50% follows from the calibration
span.quote: The threshold time was defined as the duration of the cue stimulus determining about 50% of correct stimulus detections within a series of 10 trials

span.label: SHAM rTMS delivered at the same sites, and the effect measured as the difference between real and sham
span.note: eliminates: that the effect is the coil's noise, scalp sensation or the expectation of stimulation rather than the magnetic pulse reaching cortex
span.quote: In ‘‘Consciousness’’ experiment, number of consciously perceived visual stimuli was lower by about 10% after rTMS (300 ms, 20 Hz, motor threshold intensity) on left or right PPC than after sham (pseudo) rTMS.

span.label: the same sham-difference correlation was computed ACROSS the two experiments as a control comparison
span.note: eliminates: that a correlation between the consciousness and attention measures is a general property of the difference scores rather than a shared mechanism
span.quote: As a control, the correlation was also calculated between the difference (sham-rTMS at left or right PPC) of ‘‘seen’’ trials in the ‘‘Consciousness’’ experiment and the difference (sham-rTMS at left or right PPC) of reaction times to valid trials in the ‘‘Attentional’’ experiment.

span.label: seen trials
span.quote: Trials associated with the conscious perception of cue stimuli were defined as ‘‘seen trials

span.label: conscious perception
span.quote: Trials associated with the conscious perception of cue stimuli were defined as ‘‘seen trials

span.label: threshold time
span.quote: The threshold time was defined as the duration of the cue stimulus determining about 50% of correct stimulus detections within a series of 10 trials

span.label: correct stimulus detections
span.quote: The threshold time was defined as the duration of the cue stimulus determining about 50% of correct stimulus detections within a series of 10 trials

span.label: primary consciousness
span.quote: we used repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in 18 normal subjects to investigate whether the ventral posterior parietal cortex (PPC) plays a causal role on visuospatial attention and primary consciousness

span.label: primary consciousness, as measured - THE PERCENTAGE OF `SEEN TRIALS`: the title claims a functional role in primary consciousness and the experiment records how often a subject reported perceiving a cue at their own threshold duration, so a term from consciousness theory and a detection rate occupy the same slot
span.quote: Trials associated with the conscious perception of cue stimuli were defined as ‘‘seen trials

span.label: the threshold time - EACH SUBJECT'S OWN 50% POINT: defined as the cue duration giving about 50% correct detections over 10 trials, repeated 7 times, so the quantity is fitted per person and every later percentage is measured relative to that fit
span.quote: The threshold time was defined as the duration of the cue stimulus determining about 50% of correct stimulus detections within a series of 10 trials

span.label: the 52.9% baseline - NEAR THE DESIGN TARGET BY CONSTRUCTION: the calibration sets each subject near 50% detection, so the baseline seen-trial rate is close to the number the procedure aimed at; the rTMS effect is a departure from a value the method placed there, not from a natural rate
span.quote: Across subjects mean percentage of the ‘‘seen trials’’ was 52.9% (±0.8 SE) in the baseline condition (no rTMS)

span.label: builds-on → Babiloni and others 2006
span.quote: The length of the rTMS train corresponded to the activation timing of PPC previously found in an electroencephalography (EEG) study carried out with the same paradigm (Babiloni and others 2006).

span.label: replicates → Vallar 2001; Corbetta and Shulman 2002; Karnath and others 2003; Corbetta and others 2005
span.quote: These results corroborate the well-known notion that ventral PPC is a putative substrate of neglect and other visuospatial deficits (e.g., Vallar 2001; Corbetta and Shulman 2002; Karnath and others 2003; Corbetta and others 2005).

span.label: contradicts → the idea that visuospatial attention and primary consciousness are subserved by strictly interdependent networks
span.quote: In this sense, the present findings challenge the idea that visuospatial attention and primary consciousness are subserved by strictly interdependent networks.

span.label: conscious perception —operationalised-as→ seen trials
span.quote: Trials associated with the conscious perception of cue stimuli were defined as ‘‘seen trials

span.label: threshold time —operationalised-as→ correct stimulus detections
span.quote: The threshold time was defined as the duration of the cue stimulus determining about 50% of correct stimulus detections within a series of 10 trials

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: To test the causal role of ventral PPC on primary visual consciousness (first working hypothesis; see Introduction), an analysis of variance (ANOVA) test included factor Site of Stimulation (real left PPC, real right PPC, sham) and number of ‘‘seen’’ trials as a dependent variable.

span.label: post hoc multiple comparison test
span.quote: Duncan test was used for post hoc comparisons between sham andreal rTMS conditions (P < 0.05).

span.label: correlation
span.quote: we evaluated the linear correlation of the number of ‘‘seen’’ trials in the ‘‘Consciousness’’ experiment with the reaction time in the ‘‘Attentional’’ experiment (Pearson test; Bonferroni corrected, P < 0.05).

span.label: F-test / p-value
span.quote: There was a statistically significant main effect (F2,34 = 3.77; P < 0.03; left side of Fig. 3).

span.label: mean and standard error
span.quote: Across subjects mean percentage of the ‘‘seen trials’’ was 52.9% (±0.8 SE) in the baseline condition (no rTMS), 52.2% (±0.6 SE) in the sham condition (pseudo rTMS), 44.4% (±1.9 SE) after rTMS at left PPC, and 45.9% (±1.7 SE) after rTMS at right PPC.

span.label: Repetitive TMS over either left or right ventral posterior parietal cortex significantly reduced the number of cue stimuli that subjects consciously reported seeing, compared with sham stimulation.
span.quote: Compared with the sham condition, the number of ‘‘seen’’ trials was significantly reduced after rTMS at both left (P < 0.02) and right PPC (P < 0.04), reflecting the reduction of primary visual consciousness.

span.label: The same parietal stimulation slowed reaction times to go stimuli relative to sham, indicating an impairment of covert visuospatial attention.
span.quote: With respect to the sham, the real rTMS of right or left ventral PPC slowed reaction time to go stimuli.

span.label: The size of the consciousness impairment and the size of the attention impairment were not correlated across individuals.
span.quote: First row of Figure 4 shows no statistically significant correlation (rTMS at left PPC: r = –0.36, P = 0.13; rTMS at right PPC: r = –0.18, P = 0.46).

span.label: Delivering any rTMS, real or sham, speeded reaction times relative to the no-stimulation baseline, so the attentional cost had to be measured against sham rather than baseline.
span.quote: The presence of rTMS, either real or sham, generally shortened reaction times: 418 ms (±10 SE) in the sham condition (pseudo rTMS), 446 ms (±12 SE) after rTMS at left PPC, and 438 ms (±11 SE) after rTMS at right PPC.

span.label: A control analysis validated the subjective reports: reaction times were faster on trials the subject called 'seen' than on trials called 'not seen'.
span.quote: According to the control hypothesis, mean reaction time was shorter in the ‘‘seen’’ trials than in the ‘‘not seen’’ ones regardless the spatial congruency between cue and go stimuli, thus demonstrating the global positive effect of conscious visual perception.

span.label: visual primary consciousness (operational definition)
span.quote: As a simple operational definition, here ‘‘visual primary consciousness’’ was considered as the process underlying immediate subject’s self-report about an adequate visual stimulation given to himself or herself.

span.label: primary consciousness
span.quote: Primary consciousness is an early process by which a conscious perceptive image of a sensory stimulus emerges by cortical activity, as opposed to parallel not conscious, automatic processing of the same stimulus.

span.label: threshold time (of the cue stimulus)
span.quote: The threshold time was defined as the duration of the cue stimulus determining about 50% of correct stimulus detections within a series of 10 trials, in the majority of the 7 repetitions of the procedure.

span.label: reaction time
span.quote: The reaction time for each trial class was defined as the period between the onset of the go stimulus and the mouse button click.

span.label: Site of Stimulation (real left PPC, real right PPC, sham)
span.term: Site of Stimulation (real left PPC, real right PPC, sham)
span.quote: To test the causal role of ventral PPC on visual attention (second working hypothesis), an ANOVA test included factor Site of Stimulation (real left PPC, real right PPC, sham) and reaction time in milliseconds as a dependent variable.

span.label: number of 'seen' trials (consciously perceived cue stimuli)
span.term: number of 'seen' trials (consciously perceived cue stimuli)
span.quote: To test the causal role of ventral PPC on primary visual consciousness (first working hypothesis; see Introduction), an analysis of variance (ANOVA) test included factor Site of Stimulation (real left PPC, real right PPC, sham) and number of ‘‘seen’’ trials as a dependent variable.

span.label: reaction time to the go stimulus
span.term: reaction time to the go stimulus
span.quote: The reaction time for each trial class was defined as the period between the onset of the go stimulus and the mouse button click.

span.label: sham (pseudo) rTMS block
span.quote: Finally, there was a block in which the rTMS coil was centered at scalp vertex, but it was held perpendicularly to the scalp surface (sham condition).

span.label: spatial congruence between cue and go stimulus
span.term: spatial congruence between cue and go stimulus
span.quote: which included factors Condition (‘‘seen’’ trials, ‘‘not seen’’ trials), Side of the cue stimulus (right, left), and Congruence (spatial congruence between cue stimulus and subsequent go stimulus; spatial incongruence between cue stimulus and subsequent go stimulus).

span.label: 18 — number of healthy adult volunteers stimulated
span.quote: Experiments were performed on 18 healthy adult volunteers (with ages spanning from 20 to 40 years).

span.label: about 10% — drop in the number of consciously perceived visual stimuli after parietal rTMS versus sham
span.quote: In ‘‘Consciousness’’ experiment, number of consciously perceived visual stimuli was lower by about 10% after rTMS (300 ms, 20 Hz, motor threshold intensity) on left or right PPC than after sham (pseudo) rTMS.

span.label: about 25 ms — slowing of reaction time to go stimuli caused by parietal rTMS relative to sham
span.quote: Compared with sham condition, parietal rTMS slowed of about 25 ms reaction time to go stimuli, thus disclosing effects on endogenous covert spatial attention.

span.label: 72 ms (±7.9 SE) — mean individually determined perceptive threshold duration of the cue stimulus
span.quote: Subject-by-subject, the mean threshold time of the cue stimulus was 72 ms (±7.9 SE).

span.label: F2,34 = 5.25; P < 0.01 — ANOVA main effect of stimulation site on reaction time in the Attentional experiment
span.quote: There was a statistically significant main effect (F2,34 = 5.25; P < 0.01; right side of Fig. 3).

span.label: r = –0.36, P = 0.13 — correlation between seen-trial count and reaction time after left-PPC rTMS (not significant)
span.quote: First row of Figure 4 shows no statistically significant correlation (rTMS at left PPC: r = –0.36, P = 0.13; rTMS at right PPC: r = –0.18, P = 0.46).

span.label: F1,18 = 5.84; P < 0.025 — control-ANOVA main effect of seen/not-seen condition on reaction time
span.quote: The results showed statistically significant main factors Condition (F1,18 = 5.84; P < 0.025) and Congruence (F1,18 = 5.16; P < 0.035).
